1: # CLAUDE.md
2: 
3: This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.
4: 
5: ## What this repository is
6: 
7: COMP-512 (Distributed Systems, McGill, Fall 2026) Programming Assignment 1: a Travel
8: Reservation system (flights, cars, rooms, customers) that starts as a single-process RMI
9: client/server and must be distributed two ways:
10: 
11: 1. **RMI**: client → Middleware → three per-type ResourceManagers (flights/cars/rooms).
12: 2. **TCP sockets**: same three-tier architecture, but hand-rolled sockets instead of RMI;
13:    the client stays blocking, but the Middleware and ResourceManagers must handle
14:    requests concurrently/non-blockingly.
15: 
16: Spec: `COMP512-p1-2026.pdf`. Setup walkthrough: `GettingStarted.pdf`. Client command
17: syntax: `clientUserGuide.pdf`. All working code lives under `Template/`.
18: 
19: ## Assignment-specific constraints (read before generating code here)
20: 
21: - This repo currently reflects the state where the group is using AI on the **RMI**
22:   portion. Per the spec, that requires: max ~1 day of solo work before merging with a
23:   partner's independently-built (no-AI) solution, and a full export of the AI
24:   conversation (attached to the report, with a token-usage estimate).
25: - For the **TCP sockets** portion, if AI is used, the request/response
26:   wrapping-and-dispatch logic must be implemented as one general, reusable
27:   method/service shared across (nearly) all client-callable operations — not
28:   duplicated per command.
29: - The client (`Client/Client/Client.java`, `Command.java`) must not be modified for the
30:   RMI distribution task — all changes happen server-side (Middleware + ResourceManagers).
31: 
32: ## Build & run commands
33: 
34: Build server (from `Template/Server/`):
35: ```
36: make            # compiles Server/RMI, Server/Interface, Server/Common; also produces RMIInterface.jar
37: make clean
38: ```
39: 
40: Build client (from `Template/Client/`, depends on `../Server/RMIInterface.jar`):
41: ```
42: make
43: make clean
44: ```
45: 
46: Run (from `Template/Server/`):
47: ```
48: ./run_rmi.sh                     # starts rmiregistry on port 1099 (background)
49: ./run_server.sh [<rmi_name>]     # starts one RMIResourceManager, e.g. ./run_server.sh Resources
50: ./run_servers.sh                 # tmux/ssh convenience script for launching Flights/Cars/Rooms + middleware
51:                                   #   across 4 machines — MACHINES array must be filled in with real hostnames first
52: ./run_middleware.sh <flightsHost> <carsHost> <roomsHost>   # currently a stub; see below
53: ```
54: 
55: Run client (from `Template/Client/`):
56: ```
57: ./run_client.sh [<server_hostname> [<server_rmi_name>]]   # defaults to localhost / "Resources"
58: ```
59: 
60: There is no automated test suite. Verification is manual: pipe a newline-separated
61: sequence of commands into the client, e.g.:
62: ```
63: printf 'addcustomerid,42\naddflight,1,10,100\nreserveflight,42,1\nqueryflight,1\nquit\n' \
64:   | java -cp ../Server/RMIInterface.jar:. Client.RMIClient localhost Resources
65: ```
66: Command syntax comes from the `Command` enum (`Client/Client/Command.java`) — use
67: `AddCustomerID,<id>` instead of `AddCustomer` when scripting, since `AddCustomer`
68: returns a server-generated ID you can't know ahead of time.
69: 
70: ## Architecture
71: 
72: **Transport-agnostic core, thin transport wrapper** — this split is the pattern to
73: preserve/extend when adding the Middleware and the TCP layer:
74: - `Server/Interface/IResourceManager.java` — the full RMI `Remote` contract (all
75:   add/delete/query/reserve/bundle/getName methods).
76: - `Server/Common/ResourceManager.java` — the actual business logic, implements
77:   `IResourceManager` with **no RMI-specific code at all**. Owns an in-memory
78:   `RMHashMap m_data` keyed by string (e.g. `"flight-123"`, `"customer-42"`), guarded by
79:   `synchronized(m_data)` in `readData`/`writeData`/`removeData`. `readData` returns a
80:   clone so callers can't mutate shared state directly.
81: - `Server/RMI/RMIResourceManager.java` — extends `ResourceManager`, adds only `main()`
82:   to export the object via `UnicastRemoteObject` and bind it into the `rmiregistry`
83:   under the name `<s_rmiPrefix><serverName>` (currently `group_47_<name>`).
84: 
85: A new **Middleware** class is expected at `Server/RMI/RMIMiddleware.java` (inferred from
86: the commented-out line in `run_middleware.sh`: `Server.RMI.RMIMiddleware $1 $2 $3`). It
87: should implement `IResourceManager`, look up the three per-type RMs via
88: `LocateRegistry.getRegistry(host)` + `.lookup(...)` (same pattern as
89: `Client/Client/RMIClient.connectServer`), and dispatch each interface method to the
90: correct RM. `ResourceManager.bundle(...)` currently just `return false;` — implementing
91: bundle (reserve N flights + optional car/room at one location) and deciding where
92: customer state lives (Middleware vs. a dedicated RM vs. replicated on each RM) are the
93: two open design decisions called out in the spec — customer reservation logic
94: (`reserveItem` in `ResourceManager.java`) currently assumes the customer and the
95: reservable item live in the *same* `m_data` map, so splitting customers out changes that
96: method's shape.
97: 
98: **Data model** (`Server/Common/`):
99: - `RMItem` (abstract, `Serializable`/`Cloneable`) → `ReservableItem` (abstract; count,
100:   price, reserved, location) → `Flight` / `Car` / `Room` (each just supplies a
101:   `getKey()` format: `"flight-<num>"`, `"car-<location>"`, `"room-<location>"`, all
102:   lowercased).
103: - `Customer` (also an `RMItem`) holds an `RMHashMap` of `ReservedItem`s (its personal
104:   reservation list/bill), separate from the global reservable-item map.
105: - `RMHashMap` is just `HashMap<String, RMItem>` with a deep `clone()` and a debug
106:   `dump()`.
107: 
108: **Client** (`Client/Client/`): `Client.java` is an abstract REPL (parses lines into
109: `Command` + args, dispatches via a big `switch`); `RMIClient.java` supplies
110: `connectServer()` via RMI lookup with the same `s_rmiPrefix` convention as the server
111: side. Any new transport (TCP) needs an equivalent `Client` subclass, not a
112: `Client.java` rewrite.
113: 
114: ## Known gotchas
115: 
116: - The template's `Client/Client/Client.java` originally contained a stray literal
117:   control byte (`0x03`) embedded in a line around `arguments.elementAt(1)`, causing
118:   `illegal character: '\u0003'` on `javac`. Already fixed in this checkout; if working
119:   from a fresh extraction of `Template.tar.gz`, watch for the same error.
120: - `s_rmiPrefix` is duplicated in both `Server/Server/RMI/RMIResourceManager.java` and
121:   `Client/Client/RMIClient.java` and must match exactly (currently `"group_47_"`).
122:   Rebuild both server and client after changing it — stale `.class` files won't pick it
123:   up.
124: - Default RMI registry port is `1099`, hardcoded in `run_rmi.sh`, `RMIResourceManager.java`,
125:   and `RMIClient.java` — change all three together if avoiding a port conflict with
126:   another group on a shared machine.

Don't worry! Distributed systems can feel overwhelming at first, but once you see the pattern, it becomes very straightforward. Let's take it step by step, from the big picture down to the code.

---

### Step 0: The Big Picture (What is happening?)

In the starter code, everything is done with **Java RMI**:
- When the client calls `m_resourceManager.addFlight(1, 10, 100)`, Java RMI hides all the networking. It silently opens a connection, sends the method name and parameters, runs it on the server, and gives back `true`.

For the **TCP portion**, your job is to build that "magic" yourself using regular network sockets:
1. **Client**: Instead of calling RMI, packs `("addFlight", [1, 10, 100])` into a message object and writes it into a TCP socket.
2. **Server (or Middleware)**: Reads the message object from the socket, sees `"addFlight"`, calls `addFlight(1, 10, 100)` on the database, and writes `true` back to the socket.
3. **Client**: Reads `true` from the socket and returns it to the console.

In the final setup, you have **5 machines/programs**:
- **Client**: Where the user types commands.
- **Middleware**: The central traffic cop. It listens to clients, forwards flight commands to the Flight server, car commands to the Car server, and room commands to the Room server.
- **3 Backend ResourceManagers**: One for Flights, one for Cars, one for Rooms.

---

### The 6-Step Implementation Roadmap

We will build this incrementally. **The secret is to get 1 Client $\rightarrow$ 1 Server working over TCP first**, before adding the Middleware complexity.

```
 Milestone 1: Direct TCP (Client -> Server)
   [TCPClient] --------TCP Socket--------> [TCPResourceManager]

 Milestone 2: Distributed 3-Tier (Client -> Middleware -> 3 Servers)
   [TCPClient] ------> [TCPMiddleware] ------> [Flight RM]
                                       ------> [Car RM]
                                       ------> [Room RM]
```

---

### Step 1: Create the Message Box (`TCPMessage.java`)

When the client and server talk over TCP, what are they sending?
Rather than inventing a complicated text format, Java can send whole objects over sockets using `ObjectOutputStream` and `ObjectInputStream`.

**File to create**: `Template/Server/Server/Interface/TCPMessage.java`
*(Putting it in `Server/Interface/` makes it automatically available to both client and server jar).*

**What this file contains**:
It's just a simple Java class with:
- `String id`: A unique ID (e.g. `UUID.randomUUID().toString()`) so you know which answer belongs to which question.
- `String methodName`: The name of the function to call (e.g., `"addFlight"`, `"queryCars"`).
- `Object[] args`: The arguments (e.g., `[1, 10, 100]`).
- `Object result`: The answer from the server (e.g., `true`, or a count `5`, or a bill string).
- `Exception exception`: In case something crashes on the server, pass the error back.

**Why this is special for your grade**:
The instructions say: *if using AI, wrapping/message creation must be a general method for all commands*. Because this one `TCPMessage` class works for **every single command** (`addFlight`, `reserveCar`, `deleteRooms`, etc.), it fulfills this rule completely!

### Step 2: Create the Generic Dispatcher (`GenericDispatcher.java`)

When the server receives a `TCPMessage` with `methodName = "addFlight"` and `args = [1, 10, 100]`, how does it call that method without writing 20 huge `if-else` blocks?

**File to create**: `Template/Server/Server/Common/GenericDispatcher.java`

**What this file does**:
It uses **Java Reflection**. Given any Java object (like [`ResourceManager`](file:///C:/Users/josep/OneDrive%20-%20McGill%20University/Desktop/Semester%209/COMP512/PA1-Group47/Template/Server/Server/Common/ResourceManager.java)) and a `TCPMessage`:
1. It looks at the methods available on that object.
2. It finds the method whose name matches `message.getMethodName()` and parameter count matches `args.length`.
3. It calls `method.invoke(target, message.getArgs())`.
4. It returns the result.

This is less than 50 lines of code and allows your server to dynamically execute any method without modifying it whenever new commands are added.

**Yes, exactly 100%!** 

Both RMI and TCP perform the **exact same task** with the **exact same architecture** and the **exact same business logic**:

```
[Clients]  --->  [Middleware]  --->  [Flights RM]
                               --->  [Cars RM]
                               --->  [Rooms RM]
```

A customer reserving flight #123 does the exact same thing in both versions. The difference is solely **how the computers talk to each other across the network**:

---

### The Analogy: Taking a Taxi vs. Driving Yourself

| Feature | Java RMI (High-Level RPC) | TCP Sockets (Low-Level Networking) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **What it is** | A built-in Java "magic" system. | Raw network communication built from scratch. |
| **How a call looks** | You write `rm.addFlight(1, 10, 100)` just like a normal local method call. Java quietly handles everything underneath. | You manually create a socket, package `("addFlight", [1, 10, 100])` into bytes, send it over the wire, and read the reply. |
| **Connecting** | Handled by `rmiregistry` lookup (`s_rmiPrefix + "Flights"`). | Handled by IP address and Port (`localhost:50001`). |
| **Concurrency** | Java RMI automatically spawns hidden threads for each incoming remote call. | **You** manage the threads/thread pool (`ExecutorService`) so requests don't block each other. |
| **The "Hood"** | Everything is hidden behind Java's RMI runtime. | You are building the engine yourself. |

---

### Why does the course have you do both?

1. **RMI (Milestone 1)**: Teaches you how to architect a 3-tier distributed system (Middleware coordinating multiple specialized backends, handling distributed state, bundling transactions).
2. **TCP Sockets (Milestone 2)**: Teaches you what's actually happening "under the hood" of frameworks like RMI, gRPC, and REST APIs:
   - How message serialization works.
   - How servers handle multiple concurrent clients using threads.
   - How to build a non-blocking proxy and dispatcher.

The beauty of this design is that **all your database logic ([`ResourceManager.java`](file:///C:/Users/josep/OneDrive%20-%20McGill%20University/Desktop/Semester%209/COMP512/PA1-Group47/Template/Server/Server/Common/ResourceManager.java)) and command parser ([`Client.java`](file:///C:/Users/josep/OneDrive%20-%20McGill%20University/Desktop/Semester%209/COMP512/PA1-Group47/Template/Client/Client/Client.java)) stay completely untouched!** You are just swapping out the networking layer underneath them.

- **Non-blocking Concurrency**: Uses an asynchronous thread pool (`Executors.newCachedThreadPool()`) to handle client connections. When a client request arrives, it is processed on a worker thread and forwarded without stalling the accept loop or blocking other clients.
- **Local Customer State**: Extends [`ResourceManager`](file:///C:/Users/josep/OneDrive%20-%20McGill%20University/Desktop/Semester%209/COMP512/PA1-Group47/Template/Server/Server/Common/ResourceManager.java) to store customer accounts directly at the Middleware.

- **Atomic `bundle(...)` with Rollback**: Reserves all requested flights, car, and room. If any item is unavailable or an error occurs, it rolls back all previously acquired items using `unreserveResource` and returns `false`.

#!/bin/bash 

# TODO: SPECIFY THE HOSTNAMES OF 4 CS MACHINES (tr-open-01, tr-open-02, etc...)
# For local testing, you can leave it empty or use: MACHINES=(localhost localhost localhost localhost)
MACHINES=()

PORT_FLIGHTS=50001
PORT_CARS=50002
PORT_ROOMS=50003
PORT_MW=50000

# Default to localhost if no machines specified
if [ ${#MACHINES[@]} -eq 0 ]; then
	MACHINES=(localhost localhost localhost localhost)
fi

# Build commands depending on whether running locally or via SSH
build_cmd() {
	local host=$1
	local cmd=$2
	if [ "$host" = "localhost" ] || [ "$host" = "127.0.0.1" ]; then
		echo "cd $(pwd) > /dev/null; echo -n 'Running on '; hostname; $cmd"
	else
		echo "ssh -t $host \"cd $(pwd) > /dev/null; echo -n 'Connected to '; hostname; $cmd\""
	fi
}

CMD_FLIGHTS=$(build_cmd "${MACHINES[0]}" "./run_server_tcp.sh Flights ${PORT_FLIGHTS}")
CMD_CARS=$(build_cmd "${MACHINES[1]}" "./run_server_tcp.sh Cars ${PORT_CARS}")
CMD_ROOMS=$(build_cmd "${MACHINES[2]}" "./run_server_tcp.sh Rooms ${PORT_ROOMS}")

There are **two very common reasons** this happens on McGill CS machines:

---

### 1. Check for a Comma in your `MACHINES` array (Most Likely)

Look closely at your terminal output from earlier:
```text
ssh -t tr-open-02, "cd /home/2023/jciara2/...
                 ^
                 notice the comma!
```

In Bash, array elements must be **separated by spaces, NOT commas**:

❌ **Incorrect (includes the comma in the hostname):**
```bash
MACHINES=(tr-open-01, tr-open-02, tr-open-03, tr-open-04)
```
SSH tries to connect to `tr-open-01,` (with a literal comma) and fails with:
`ssh: Could not resolve hostname tr-open-01,: Name or service not known`

✅ **Correct (separated by spaces only):**
```bash
MACHINES=(tr-open-01 tr-open-02 tr-open-03 tr-open-04)
```

---

### 2. The Machine is Offline or Crashed

As noted in `GettingStarted.pdf`:
> *"You should be able to use the following machines located in Trottier building... (note that some may be offline or have crashed - you must check which ones are available)."*

The `tr-open-*` nodes are physical lab workstations in the Trottier building. Students frequently reboot them into Windows or turn them off.

#### How to test which machines are alive:
